title: Control Flow
objectives: Write switch statements with correct break usage

content.heading: if / else
content.body: C's if (condition) { ... } else if (condition) { ... } else { ... } treats any non-zero value as true and zero as false for condition — this is why if (someInt) is common idiomatic C for 'if someInt is non-zero', and why C historically had no distinct boolean type. Nested if statements work exactly as expected, though deeply nested conditionals are, as in any language, often a sign the logic could be restructured for clarity.

content.heading: switch, case, default, and break
content.body: switch (expression) { case value1: ...; break; case value2: ...; break; default: ...; } compares expression (which must be an integer type — int, char, or an enum, never a float or string) against each case label. Without an explicit break, execution falls through into the following case's code regardless of its label — a deliberate C language feature (occasionally useful for intentionally grouping multiple case labels with shared behavior) but a very common source of bugs when a break is simply forgotten. default handles any value matching no explicit case, and can appear anywhere in the switch (though conventionally placed last).

content.explanation: case 1: falling through into case 7: (with no break between them) intentionally treats both labels the same way — a legitimate, deliberate use of fall-through, distinct from accidentally forgetting a break.

keyPoints: Any non-zero value is treated as true in a C condition; zero is false
switch only accepts integer-family expressions (int, char, enum) — not float or string
Without break, execution falls through to the next case's code
default handles values matched by no explicit case
commonMistakes: Forgetting break in a switch case, causing unintended fall-through
Using = instead of == inside an if condition, silently assigning instead of comparing
Trying to switch on a float or a string, neither of which switch supports
